analysis.one_liner: Makes employers keep records and give notices classifying workers as employees or contractors, with new penalties for misclassification.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or floor action; it died in the Senate committee it was referred to when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: Companies sometimes label workers as independent contractors instead of employees, which lets the companies skip minimum wage, overtime, and payroll contributions. This bill would have required every employer to keep records stating each worker's classification, give workers a written notice of their classification and their rights, double back-pay damages when a wage violation involves misclassification, fine repeat violators up to $10,000 per violation, and push states to audit employers who misclassify workers to keep them off unemployment coverage.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers misclassified as independent contractors, who would gain clearer notice of their status, an easier path to minimum wage and overtime claims, doubled damages when misclassification is part of a wage violation, and better access to unemployment insurance; honest employers who already classify correctly would face less underpricing from competitors who misclassify.

how_it_helps.text: Every employer would have to keep records of non-employees performing labor and record an accurate classification of each worker as an employee or non-employee [S3].

Employers would have to give each worker a written notice stating how they are classified, directing them to a Department of Labor rights website, and telling workers suspected of misclassification to contact the Department of Labor [S3].

Failing to accurately classify a worker would become a prohibited act, and liquidated damages for minimum wage and maximum hours violations would double when the employer also misclassified the worker [S3].
Employers who repeatedly or willfully violate the notice rules would face a civil penalty of up to $10,000 per violation [S3].

States would have to run audit programs identifying employers whose misclassification excludes workers from unemployment compensation, and set administrative penalties for misclassification, as a condition of federal unemployment grants [S2] [S3].
The Department of Labor would have to focus at least 25% of Wage and Hour Division audits on misclassification recordkeeping, aimed at industries with frequent misclassification [S3].

The Labor Department would have to build a plain-language website summarizing workers' rights, in English and other prevalent languages, and share misclassification findings internally, with referral to the IRS allowed [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers that use independent contractors would bear new recordkeeping and notice costs, exposure to doubled damages, fines up to $10,000 per violation, and a higher chance of audit; some workers classified as contractors would lose arrangements if employers reclassified or cut them to avoid the new liabilities.

drawbacks.text: The recordkeeping and notice requirements would add paperwork and compliance costs to every employer, not just those violating the law [S3].
Doubled damages and per-violation penalties could push some firms to stop using contractors altogether rather than reclassify, costing flexible workers their engagements [S3].

Sharing misclassification information with the IRS expands data-sharing between labor and tax enforcement agencies, which critics of employment-tax enforcement could object to on privacy and burden grounds [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The compliance costs fall on all employers, but the bill targets a specific practice — misclassifying employees as contractors to avoid wage, hour, and payroll obligations — that shifts costs onto workers and onto compliant competitors. The worker-side benefits (notice, doubled damages, unemployment coverage) are targeted at people who currently have no easy way to challenge their classification.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in late September 2008 and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never acted on it before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

narrative.text: Sen. Edward Kennedy introduced the bill in the Senate on September 29, 2008 [S1] [S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day [S5].
No further action — no committee markup, no floor vote, no House action — appears in the bill's action history before the Congress ended [S5].
The bill was introduced weeks before a presidential election and during the 2008 financial crisis, near the end of the two-year session, leaving almost no runway for committee work [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that classify workers as independent contractors avoided new recordkeeping duties, doubled wage damages, and fines of up to $10,000 per violation. Workers misclassified by those employers gained nothing from this Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never advanced far enough to draw recorded votes or floor opposition; all three sponsors were Democrats, but no roll-call or committee vote shows where opposition came from.

industries.industry: Employers that rely on independent contractors (staffing, construction, trucking, services)
industries.note: These firms would face recordkeeping and notice duties, doubled wage damages, and $10,000-per-violation fines, and 25% of Labor Department audits would target misclassification-heavy industries. Misclassification lets such employers skip minimum wage, overtime, and payroll contributions, a cost borne by workers.

industries.industry: Payroll processing and employment-tax compliance businesses
industries.note: New recordkeeping, classification notice, and state unemployment-audit requirements would create demand for compliance and payroll services.
